n: Five days later the high priest came to Caesarea with elders and a professional lawyer, Tertullus, to press charges against Paul before Governor Felix.

f.g: A professional advocate or attorney skilled in Roman legal speech.

n: Tertullus opened with lavish flattery, praising Felix for bringing peace and reforms. In reality Felix’s rule was marked by unrest and brutality.

f.g: Peace — Felix had violently suppressed rebel groups.

n: More flattery: we gratefully acknowledge your benefits everywhere, most excellent Felix.
Not wanting to take too much of your time, he said, please kindly hear us briefly.
Tertullus brings three charges: Paul is a public menace, a stirrer of riots among Jews everywhere (a political crime Rome took seriously), and a ringleader of the Nazarene sect.

f.g: A name for Christians, after Jesus of Nazareth.

n: The fourth charge: Paul tried to desecrate the temple. They claimed they arrested him to judge him by their law — leaving out that they had been beating him.
Tertullus blames the commander Lysias for using violence to take Paul. Many ancient manuscripts omit the end of verse 6 through the start of verse 8.

f.g: A distorted account — Lysias had rescued Paul from a mob.

n: If you examine him yourself, Tertullus says, you will confirm our accusations.
The Jewish leaders present joined in, insisting the charges were true.
At Felix’s signal, Paul responded — courteously but without flattery — saying he gladly made his defense before someone who had judged this nation for years and knew its customs.
Only twelve days earlier he had come to Jerusalem to worship — hardly time to organize a rebellion.
No one had found him arguing in the temple or stirring up crowds anywhere — not in synagogues or the city.
They have no proof for their charges.
But Paul freely admits one thing: he worships the God of his ancestors according to “the Way,” which they call a sect, believing everything in the law and the prophets.

f.g: Greek hairesis — a sect or party; the same word used for the Pharisees and Sadducees.

f.w: believing all things which are written

n: He shares their hope in God that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.

f.w: a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust

n: So he strives always to keep a clear conscience before God and people. Paul’s life matches his beliefs.
After years away, he came to Jerusalem bringing gifts for the poor of his nation and offerings — the collection from the Gentile churches.

f.w: to bring alms to my nation

n: While doing this, he was ritually purified in the temple — not with a crowd or causing trouble — when some Jews from Asia found him.
Those Asian Jews, his original accusers, should be here to make their charges in person. Roman law frowned on accusers who failed to appear.
Or let these men here say what wrongdoing they found when he stood before the Sanhedrin.
Unless, Paul adds pointedly, it was the one thing he shouted: that he is on trial for believing in the resurrection of the dead.

f.w: Touching the resurrection of the dead

n: Felix, who knew a good deal about “the Way,” postponed a decision until Lysias could come. In practice, he left Paul waiting.
He kept Paul in custody but with some freedom, allowing friends to visit and care for his needs.
Some days later, Felix and his wife Drusilla — a young Jewish princess, daughter of Herod Agrippa I — sent for Paul to hear about faith in Christ.

f.g: Daughter of Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12) and sister of Agrippa II; she had left her first husband to marry Felix.

n: As Paul spoke of righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and sent him away, promising to listen at a more convenient time. That convenient time may never have come.

f.w: when I have a convenient season

n: Felix also hoped Paul would bribe him for release, so he often sent for him and talked with him.
After two years, Porcius Festus replaced Felix as governor. To please the Jewish leaders, Felix left Paul in prison.

f.g: Paul was held in Caesarea about AD 57–59.
